entries.seminar_title: Price Discrimination and Revealed Consumer Welfare
entries.speaker: João Thereze
entries.abstract: We take a revealed-preference approach to study the welfare effects of price discrimination. An analyst observes price and quantity data before and after a monopolist segments the market. The analyst knows neither the aggregate demand curve nor the information available to the monopolist. We characterize the set of observable price-quantity pairs that are rationalizable by some market segmentation. We then obtain sharp bounds on the change in consumer surplus arising from some segmentation. Finally, we provide conditions under which the data identifies an unambiguous increase (decrease) in consumer surplus.
entries.bio: João Thereze is an Assistant Professor of Economics at Duke: Fuqua Business.

entries.seminar_title: Climate Damage Amplification: Arctic Sea Ice Loss and Storm Impacts
entries.speaker: Max Zahrah
entries.abstract: Empirical estimates of climate damages suggest that high-latitude regions stand to gain from warming. These estimates project future damages by shifting the distribution of hazards along a fixed damage function. But climate change can also alter the damage function itself by eroding the protective natural capital that reduces climate damages. Sea ice along the Alaskan coast is one such form of protective natural capital: it dampens the waves that winter storms drive onshore, and it is retreating as the Arctic warms. Since ice cover varies from storm to storm, storms of similar severity can be compared across different levels of ice protection, providing an existence proof of this amplification. Using surge and wave hindcasts matched to 2,748 storms across 28 coastal communities, I find that a one-standard-deviation increase in pre-storm sea ice (23 percentage points) reduces wave height by 45 percent. FEMA spending is roughly 60 percent lower for a high-severity storm when pre-storm ice is one standard deviation higher, though this estimate rests on a small number of FEMA-funded disasters.
entries.bio: Max Zahrah is a PhD Student in Sustainable Development at Columbia University.

entries.seminar_title: Timely Policy Responses Can Save Fisheries from (Some) Temperature Shocks
entries.speaker: Kimberly Oremus
entries.abstract: Marine heat extremes are intensifying, straining management systems designed around stable conditions. While biological effects of warming are well-documented, critical knowledge gaps remain regarding when and how policy interventions can accelerate ecological recovery. Here, we develop a temperature-dependent bioeconomic framework that identifies thresholds and quantifies trade-offs between recovery and economic performance in a blue-crab fishery across >11,000 simulated warming and policy scenarios. We find a critical ‘window of intervention’ within which policies effectively accelerate recovery, but beyond which ecological damage overwhelms regulatory capacity. Within this window, protecting reproductive capacity through targeted harvest restrictions consistently outperforms broader closures with more favorable economic outcomes. Outside this thermal threshold, even aggressive interventions prove ineffective. The seasonal timing of warming events determines intervention success, with summer extremes imposing the greatest constraints on management effectiveness. These findings demonstrate that policy cost-effectiveness varies across warming scenarios. Our framework informs how managers can compare different regulatory actions in temperature-sensitive systems.
entries.bio: Kimberly Oremus is an Associate Professor of Marine Science and Policy at the University of Delaware.
